## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Linemen and line inspectors who patrol a utility's poles.
   [HN] "Most utilities solve this problem with foot patrols. Linemen drive out with a clipboard or an iPad, and run
   through a checklist with binoculars to visually confirm everything is in order." [HN] "We're making weatherized,
   hybrid-fixed drones deployed for power utility inspections." → `roles[lineman]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Confirm every pole and line is sound before it fails.
   [HN] "But when the wood starts to rot, or the cotter pin falls out, and a live conductor is dropped on a dead tree on
   a windy day, you get devastating wildfires like the Palisades Fire in LA last year." → `context.job`,
   `statements.problem`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** On an inspection patrol, pole by pole from the ground; and reactive patrols after storms or a
   strange feeder reading.
   [HN] "A lineman can inspect about 50-150 poles per day, yet even the smallest rural electric cooperatives (with about
   ~20 employees) have about 50,000 distribution poles. Clearly the math doesn't work out. As a result, a given utility
   pole is inspected about every 10 years". [HN] "If there's a weird harmonic on a feeder, or a utility needs a rapid
   scan after a storm, we can get on-site within minutes to inspect." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: pole
   inspection patrol`. Author's choice: the window {3, MONTHS} (the research's "monthly cycle" rhythm; spec 120 reads a
   monthly rhythm as 3 MONTHS), Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most": not every lineman is put
   on patrols in a quarter; storm and construction crews may not be).

4. **Which people.** Linemen and inspectors at US electric utilities and rural co-ops.
   [HN] "The U.S. has 7M miles of power lines (enough to go to the moon and back 14 times), and they're aging." [HN]
   "Power utilities are our first customers". → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The utility, per pole or tower inspected.
   [HN] "Our business model is straightforward: inspection as a service. We charge per pole or tower." [HN] "We just
   secured our first major contract and are working out the details of pilots with some big utilities. Our first paid
   flight is mid-April." [LYC1] "If you're interested in piloting our service, reach out to avi@voltairlabs.com" →
   `persona.decision_maker: {role: manager}`. Author's choice: the decider is the utility's inspection manager and the
   tested role "The VP of operations" (with "The co-op board" listed): no public source names a buyer title. Purchase
   friction's tested item "An FAA waiver to fly beyond sight" is from [HN] (avigotskind, a founder): "There's no real
   way around BVLOS regs right now. The real problem is BVLOS + need to recharge." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444564 ;
   the pad safety review is from [HN] "The risk of landing a drone multiple times per day at myriad points around the
   network felt too risky for utility engineers."; the competitive bid is the author's. Commitment's step "pay for a
   pilot on one feeder": [HN] "Our first paid flight is mid-April"; "on one feeder" is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Fixed-wing drones that live outside and recharge on pads along the lines.
   [HN] "We're making weatherized, long-range (well over 70 miles), fixed-wing drones that can live outside for months
   at a time. They recharge inductively (no connections or moving parts) on stripped-down charging pads that cost a
   couple thousand dollars apiece." [HN] "we use the charging station as an intermediary, dumping the data from our
   drone to a hard drive on the station over a high-speed WiFi link." [HN] (wweissbluth, a founder) "We're collecting
   61MP RGB, LiDAR (DSM DTM) and radiometric thermal for sensors" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444631 .
   The earlier idea, dropped before the HN post: [LYC1] "We build drones that charge directly on transmission lines."
   and [HN] "There's not enough current on distribution lines!" → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`.
   Compatibility (pole tops visible from above — tested; a spot for a pad; findings into the work order system) and
   Adoption friction (review the drone's flags before sending crews — tested; work from a defect list) are the
   author's, from the mechanism's needs. Relative advantage: [HN] "Xcel power found drones to find 60% more defects than
   foot patrols (because of pole-top vantage point)" (less_worry) and the 50-150 poles a day (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.**
   Price: **the operator's reading.** [HN] gives the unit only ("We charge per pole or tower"); no amount appears in any
   launch-era or later source. The founder's price is set at **$3 to $5 per pole, each**, below the author's estimate
   of the foot patrol's cost per pole, since the founders sell on cost ([HN] "Georgia Power saved 60% on operating
   expenses when they switched to using drones"). Under the engine's `compare` reading the founder's ratio is 30% to
   125% of the cost (CommercialChain.derive).
   Cost, MONEY **$4 to $10 of the pole inspections per pole, each**: author's arithmetic. A lineman's day of 8 hours at
   [BLS] "The median annual wage for electrical power-line installers and repairers was $95,320 in May 2025" ($45.83 an
   hour) is about $367; with a truck and fuel, about $500 a day; over [HN]'s 50-150 poles a day, $3.30 to $10 a pole,
   taken as $4 to $10. The helicopter ($25k a flight) and the drone-in-a-box ($250,000 a box) are left as the founders'
   comparisons in the statement, not folded into the per-pole cost.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (Uncle_Clark) "I work for a utility company and this is brilliant. One other issue that comes into play for
   inspections is right of way." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47446642 ; [HN] (lifis) "Why not just install
   cameras on the poles?" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47452396 ; [HN] (petargyurov, who builds analytics on
   drone and helicopter imagery) "This is a tough problem to solve and for a lot of operators ultimately comes down to
   cost." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444350 . No first-person lineman account exists in the sources.

## Status today

Widened in pitch, same buyer. [YCP] today reads "Autonomous Drones for Earth Observation", with power utilities "the
perfect first customer" ([LYC2] 2026-03-13: "Power utilities are the perfect first customer. ... Voltair can serve
existing multi-billion dollar data markets in road, rail and telecom inspection at 10x lower prices"). [SITE] still sells
utility inspection only ("Voltair | Autonomous Drone Inspection for Electric Utilities"), with charging moved to
"Ground infrastructure at utility substations", and offers a pilot slot. Price today: none public ([SITE], read
2026-10-22: no price or per-pole figure).

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price amount.** Never published, at launch or since; the founder's $3 to $5 per pole is the operator's reading
  (item 7), and the header says so.
- **The cost per pole.** The founders give poles a day, not dollars; $4 to $10 is the author's arithmetic on [BLS].
- **Volumes.** How many poles a utility inspects a year is not asked by Keel (no volume question on `each`); the
  50,000-pole co-op is in the statement only.
- **A buyer title** and every Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment item beyond those quoted in item 5.
- **First-person lineman accounts.** None in the sources; the stories are scripted from the founders' post and the
  thread.
- **Which launch statement is "day one".** [LYC1] (2026-01-23) pitched power-line charging; the entry uses [HN]
  (2026-03-19), where that approach is dropped, as the idea the founders held at launch.

insights.line: What it would have to do better

whys.g1: The two answers say different things — Ray names the bar it would have to clear (catch what our own checks miss) while Keisha says patrols aren't the problem at all, trouble calls and short crews are — so leaving each on its own is how I'd sort them, and there's no existing group either one was wrongly kept out of.
whys.g2: There's no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line — Keisha's answer is about where her week actually goes, which is a fair reply to what it would have to do better — and nothing was grouped that shouldn't be.

PRIMARY.order_why: It goes from whether I'm in the trade, to whether this happened to me, to whether it fits, what blocks it, whether it's better, what it takes to start, and whether I'd try it, which is the order I'd think it through.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 6 overlap: 'what would get in the way' and 'could you start without much trouble' both ask what stands between me and using it.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked whether a drone can even see my poles. A lot of my circuit runs under timber where you can't see the pole tops from above. They also didn't ask about the groundline checks I do by sounding and boring for rot, which a drone flying overhead can't do.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' is plain, but the number that decides it (the worst card, Relative advantage at 4 of 6, right on the bar) is not beside it, and the added 'more said yes than you thought' describes the two better cards, not the deciding one.
screens.why_b2: Each card's line says what was counted (said yes), over how many (6), and where my bar sits (4 of 6), so I can read all three at once.
screens.why_b3: The three dimensions are mine and the belief lines are recognisable, but they are stiff templates ('confirming every pole and line is sound before it fails this way, with Voltair'), and the statement under the title is garbled ('Linemen and line inspectors Weatherized, long-range...' and '. and gets back')
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what to do next: not to probe why only 4 of 6 found it better than the foot patrol, and not whether to take the pilot pitch to utilities.
screens.why_b5: The 6-of-7 count is visible, but the headline 'more said yes than you thought' oversells a verdict whose deciding card scraped the bar at 4 of 6, and the page never says that six linemen is a thin read or why one answer was not counted.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: better than today sits right on your bar (4 of 6). Fit and getting started cleared it (5 of 6). Only 6 linemen were counted, so before pitching the pilot, open Relative advantage and find out what the two who said no do instead.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 6 said yes · bar 4 of 6', so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: What is counted (said yes) and over how many (6) are plain, but the chart's axis runs in tenths while the bar is given as '4 of 6' and my belief as '6 to 7 in 10', so I have to convert between scales to see where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Voltair, and my own job line 'confirming every pole and line is sound before it fails' are the words I typed, even if 'this way' is clunky.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats '5 of 6 said yes'; Travis's timber quote is the one concrete lead (lines under canopy, where tops can't be seen from above), but the screen never says what that means for which feeders to pilot on.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the headline 'more said yes than you thought' reads as stronger than six people can carry, since one person is all that separates 5 of 6 from my band.
screens.instead: Holding up: 5 of 6 linemen said it fits how they work (your bar was 4 of 6), only six people, so a lean; the one No was a line under thick timber where pole tops can't be seen from above, so check canopy cover before picking pilot feeders.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "4 of 6 said yes · bar 4 of 6 · at the bar", so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it at once.

screens.why7: It is Yes then No on the one measure of fit, names the brand and the job in the -ing form, has no escape as the card requires, and can go either way.

screens.why1: Right after I said Voltair wouldn't fit how I work, asking what would stop it is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but it doesn't say in the way of what, so I have to carry over Voltair and my answer from the last screen myself.
screens.why3: I can answer from my own patrols: half my line runs under timber and you can't see the pole tops from above, so I'd say that straight off.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options or chips.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan or terms comes through; it just asks what would stop it fitting my work.
screens.why6: Six words and one question, easy to hear once and answer out loud.
screens.instead: You said it wouldn't fit how you check your poles. What would get in the way of using Voltair on your lines?

screens.why1: Right after I said whether Voltair would fit how I work and what would get in the way, it makes sense to ask whether it would beat how I do it now.
screens.why2: I'd answer it, but 'confirm every pole and line is sound before it fails' isn't how we talk; we say we inspect or patrol the line, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I walk and inspect poles on my circuits now, so I can compare that with what I was shown, even if my answer is no because the line runs under timber.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, nothing overlaps, and the card calls for no escape here.
screens.why5: Voltair shown by name after the idea is fine, but the job is the founder's wording, not a lineman's, so it drifts a little from how I'd say it.
screens.why6: It's one question with an easy 'Yes or no', but it runs right to 20 words and 'is sound before it fails today' is a mouthful, with 'today' left dangling at the end.
screens.why7: There's one measure, better than my way today, with Yes for and No against, no escape as the card requires, and none of the founder's benefits offered as options.
screens.instead: Compared with the way you inspect your poles and lines today, would Voltair be better? Yes · No

screens.why1: After asking whether Voltair would fit and whether it would be better, it makes sense to ask whether I could actually get started with it.
screens.why2: Poles, flags and crews are all words I use, and I get it on the first read or hearing.
screens.why3: I could look over poles a drone flagged, but deciding when to send crews is usually the foreman's or the engineer's call, not mine, so I'd half be guessing for someone else.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, they don't overlap, and with this card a missing escape is right.
screens.why5: The drone flagging poles is what the idea card already showed me, so nothing new about the product slips through, and it reads like the founder's setup step.
screens.why6: It's one short setup sentence and one question, ending on 'yes or no', easy to hold after one hearing.
screens.why7: Yes and No sit on the one measure as the card asks, but reviewing flagged poles is really using the tool rather than a setup I'd do before first use, and 'before sending crews' brings in a dispatch step that's someone else's, so the setup rule is bent.
screens.instead: Before you could use Voltair for this, you would need to check the poles a drone flags on your circuit. Could you start without much trouble? Yes · No

screens.why1: It's the last question after I've heard what Voltair is and said whether it fits, so asking if I'd actually try it makes sense here.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but 'try it for real' leaves me guessing what I'd be signing up for: flying it on my circuit, sitting through a demo, or my co-op buying it.
screens.why3: I patrol the poles, but whether a drone program gets used on our lines is the utility's or co-op's call, so I'd be guessing about my own part in it.
screens.why4: Yes and No are clean, but for a lineman the true answer is often 'not my call, my supervisor decides', and that isn't there.
screens.why5: Voltair was shown to me on purpose earlier in the study, and nothing new from the founder's plan or terms comes through here.
screens.why6: It's one short question with two options, easy to hear once and answer, though 'I'll read 2 options' for a yes or no is a bit stiff.
screens.instead: If your utility let you, would you try Voltair on the next circuit you're due to patrol? Yes; No; or it's not my call.
